overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how Descartes and Kant framed the relation between the knowing subject and the world. You'll be asked about the method of doubt and the cogito, the wax example, Kant's forms of intuition, and the distinction between phenomena and things in themselves.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Descartes introduce the supposition of a malicious demon in the First Meditation?

options.html: To prove that the external world does not exist
options.text: To prove that the external world does not exist
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Descartes doesn't claim the world doesn't exist. The demon extends his method of doubt, so he can set aside every belief that admits any doubt at all, including beliefs about the world and his own body.

options.html: To extend doubt to every belief that admits the slightest doubt
options.text: To extend doubt to every belief that admits the slightest doubt
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The demon is a methodological device. By supposing a powerful deceiver, Descartes can suspend even beliefs that survive the dream argument, so that only what is truly certain remains.

options.html: To show that the senses deceive only about distant objects
options.text: To show that the senses deceive only about distant objects
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That the senses sometimes mislead about small or distant things is the first, narrowest stage of doubt. The demon is introduced to extend doubt to every belief that admits the slightest doubt.

options.html: To explain how dreams arise from bodily causes
options.text: To explain how dreams arise from bodily causes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Descartes doesn't explain dreams causally. The demon is introduced to extend doubt to every belief that admits the slightest doubt, beyond what the dream argument reaches.

forms.stemHtml: Why does the claim "I am, I exist" survive even the supposition of a deceiving demon?

options.html: Because the senses reliably confirm the existence of one's own body
options.text: Because the senses reliably confirm the existence of one's own body
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Descartes has already set aside the senses and the body as doubtful. "I am, I exist" survives because being deceived, or thinking at all, requires that the one thinking exists.

options.html: Because God guarantees that clear and simple beliefs are true
options.text: Because God guarantees that clear and simple beliefs are true
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. At this point, Descartes hasn't appealed to God to secure anything. "I am, I exist" survives because being deceived, or thinking at all, requires that the one thinking exists.

options.html: Because being deceived, or thinking at all, requires that the thinker exists
options.text: Because being deceived, or thinking at all, requires that the thinker exists
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! However powerful the deceiver, it can't make Descartes nothing while he thinks he is something. So "I am, I exist" is true whenever he thinks it.

options.html: Because mathematical truths remain certain whether one is awake or dreaming
options.text: Because mathematical truths remain certain whether one is awake or dreaming
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Mathematical truths survive the dream argument, but Descartes then doubts even these. "I am, I exist" survives because being deceived, or thinking at all, requires that the thinker exists.

forms.stemHtml: In Descartes's wax example, every sensible quality of the wax changes near the fire, yet the same wax remains. What does Descartes conclude?

options.html: The wax is not perceived at all, only imagined by the mind
options.text: The wax is not perceived at all, only imagined by the mind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Descartes agrees the wax is perceived throughout, and he argues that imagination can't grasp it either. He concludes that the wax is grasped by the mind alone, through something like judgment.

options.html: The wax is known through imagination, which pictures all its possible shapes
options.text: The wax is known through imagination, which pictures all its possible shapes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Descartes argues that the wax can take more shapes than imagination could ever run through. He concludes that the wax is grasped by the mind alone, through something like judgment.

options.html: The wax is known best through touch, which stays constant as it melts
options.text: The wax is known best through touch, which stays constant as it melts
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Touch changes too: the wax goes from hard and cold to liquid and hot. Descartes concludes that the wax is grasped by the mind alone, through something like judgment.

options.html: The wax is grasped by the mind alone, through something like judgment
options.text: The wax is grasped by the mind alone, through something like judgment
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Because no sensible quality stays the same, the wax's identity can't come from the senses or imagination. Descartes concludes that it is grasped by the mind alone, an early account of perception as judgment.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following does Kant treat as forms of intuition? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Space
options.text: Space
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Kant, space is the form of outer sense: everything you experience as outside you appears in space.

options.html: Causality
options.text: Causality
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Causality is one of the categories, the pure concepts of the understanding, not a form of intuition. The forms of intuition are space and time.

options.html: Time
options.text: Time
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Kant, time is the form of inner sense, so all your experiences, including perceptions of outer things, come in time.

options.html: Substance
options.text: Substance
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Substance is one of the categories, the pure concepts of the understanding, not a form of intuition. The forms of intuition are space and time.

forms.stemHtml: For Kant, objects as they appear under the conditions of experience are , and objects considered apart from those conditions can be .

options.html: phenomena
options.text: phenomena
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Phenomena, or appearances, are objects as they are given under the forms of intuition and the categories. They are the objects of all possible knowledge.

options.html: things in themselves
options.text: things in themselves
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Things in themselves are objects considered apart from the conditions of experience. Objects as they appear under those conditions are phenomena.

options.html: forms of intuition
options.text: forms of intuition
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Space and time are forms of intuition, the ways objects are given, not the objects themselves. Objects as they appear under the conditions of experience are phenomena.

options.html: known through science
options.text: known through science
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Science studies phenomena, so it doesn't give knowledge of things in themselves. For Kant, things in themselves can be thought, but not known.

options.html: thought, but not known
options.text: thought, but not known
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Kant holds that you can think of things in themselves without contradiction, but knowledge reaches only as far as possible experience.

options.html: perceived, but not thought
options.text: perceived, but not thought
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Things in themselves are never given in perception. For Kant, things in themselves can be thought, but not known.

title: Descartes, Kant, and Experience
